questions.stem: State what VSEPR stands for and what it predicts.
questions.modelAnswer: Valence shell electron pair repulsion theory, which predicts the shapes and bond angles of molecules.

questions.stem: State the repulsion order for lone and bonding pairs.
questions.modelAnswer: Strongest first: lone-with-lone, then lone-against-bond, then bond-with-bond.

questions.stem: Explain why a molecule adopts the shape it does, in VSEPR terms.
questions.modelAnswer: The electron pairs around the central atom all repel each other, so the molecule settles into the arrangement that pushes those clouds as far apart as possible - the geometry with the least total repulsion is the stable one.

questions.stem: Predict whether replacing a bonding pair with a lone pair on a central atom increases or decreases the pressure on the remaining bonds, and why.
questions.modelAnswer: It increases the pressure: the lone pair's more concentrated cloud repels harder than the bond pair it replaced, squeezing the remaining bonds closer together.

questions.stem: Define bond length.
questions.modelAnswer: Bond length is the internuclear distance of two covalently bonded atoms.

questions.stem: State which bond type is shortest and strongest, with the reason.
questions.modelAnswer: Triple bonds - their large electron density between the nuclei raises attraction, pulling the atoms closest.

questions.stem: Explain why greater electron-nucleus attraction strengthens a covalent bond.
questions.modelAnswer: Stronger attraction holds the shared electrons more firmly between the two nuclei and draws those nuclei nearer, so more energy is required to separate the bonded atoms - which is precisely a stronger bond.

questions.stem: Arrange single, double and triple bonds by increasing bond length and state the strength order that accompanies it.
questions.modelAnswer: Length: triple < double < single; strength runs the same ladder upward - triple strongest, single weakest - because density between the nuclei rises with bond order.

questions.stem: State the bond angles of linear, trigonal planar and tetrahedral shapes.
questions.modelAnswer: Linear 180 degrees, trigonal planar 120 degrees, tetrahedral 109.5 degrees.

questions.stem: State what VSEPR pairs with every molecular shape it names.
questions.modelAnswer: Each shape carries its corresponding bond angles - the catalogue pairs shape with angle.

questions.stem: Explain why four electron domains settle at 109.5 degrees rather than 120.
questions.modelAnswer: Four clouds cannot fit in one plane; they spread into three dimensions, pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron whose interior angles - 109.5 degrees - minimise the mutual repulsion.

questions.stem: A molecule shows three electron domains around its central atom. Predict its shape and bond angle via the catalogue.
questions.modelAnswer: Three domains spread in one plane: trigonal planar shape with 120 degree bond angles.
